summary: A satirical piece about Redfield City's attempt, launched by Mayor Julius Green on September 5, 2023, to overhaul public service delivery. Each initiative, from e-government to transparency, accountability, customer service, decision-making, citizen engagement, streamlining, budgeting, smart city tech and pilot projects, is shown failing in absurd ways. It ends by questioning whether the officials can escape the administrative maze they created.
one_line: Satire of Redfield City's string of failed public service reform initiatives under Mayor Julius Green, from e-government to smart city pilots.
key_facts: Mayor Julius Green launched a strategic revamp of public service delivery in Redfield City on September 5, 2023.
Redfield City's population has crossed the half-million mark.
The kickoff meetings were scheduled to begin with the 'Department for Expedited Services', whose processing time is likened to continental drift.
On September 15, Councilwoman Jennifer Strauss introduced digital services; when City Manager Arnold Fumble clicked 'enter', the website displayed 'Page Not Found'.
The 'Transparency Initiative' released a flurry of densely detailed documents on October 1, causing more confusion than clarity.

Deputy Mayor Linda Brushwood introduced the Redfield Accountability Framework at an October press conference; its complex responsibility-tracing mechanism was overtaken by public interest in a cat resembling the Mayor.
Customer service czar Mr. Harry Bottleneck announced 'No citizen left behind' in November; the new center's ticketing system accidentally issued all visitors the same number.
The Dartboard Method for decision-making launched December 6, using a board that spins at an alarming speed.
In early January the planning department held citizen workshops featuring pre-scripted 'feedback' delivered by actors.
Streamlined processes launched in February became a 'hurdle marathon' for citizens.
In March Finance Director Ivana Cash presented the 'Doing More with Less' program, claiming decreased funds increase efficiency.
In early April the 'Smart City' transition saw the automated parking system ticket every vehicle, including bicycles and rollerblades.
April pilots included mail-delivery drones causing 'haircut-by-propeller', autonomous garbage trucks that ousted street bins, and a city-wide Wi-Fi network that mostly showed a buffering symbol.
